rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs. The high final organic fraction minimizes the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Halve the gradient slope to spread the crowded central cluster and late doublet while isolating the effect of slope. The initial run leaves substantial room to increase retention before the time penalty begins.
Keep the successful shallow gradient and test a substantial temperature change to alter selectivity at the remaining near-coelution. Higher temperature may also shorten the elution window.
Slightly flatten the gradient at 60 C to try to lift the sole remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. The last peak at 7.77 minutes leaves ample room before the time penalty.

The flatter gradient worsened the critical pair, so use a slightly steeper slope than injection 3. This intermediate slope targets R ≥ 1.5 for that pair while preserving the narrower separation margins in the earlier cluster.

Increase the slope only slightly, from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting the 1.49-resolution pair while preserving the early pairs. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, so the lower endpoint should not affect their separation.
Injection 6 achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving slope to test whether the fully resolved separation can be shortened further.
Flatten the gradient at the higher starting organic fraction to recover resolution in the early cluster while retaining some time savings. Injection 6 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Test a small temperature reduction to shift selectivity between the two marginal pairs at the higher starting organic fraction. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved method while preserving injection 6 as the maximum-CRF benchmark.

Test a larger temperature shift because the early-cluster selectivity deteriorated at 55 C, while 40 C previously separated much of that cluster well. This checks another selectivity regime for a faster fully resolved method; injection 6 already secures the maximum CRF.

Move below 40 C to test whether the central near-coelution separates while the other pairs retain their resolution margins. The observed elution window leaves room for the expected retention increase without a time penalty.

Test the unmeasured 45 C selectivity regime, where the central coelution seen at 40 C may separate before the early pair becomes limiting at 55 C. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate temperature effects.

Return to the maximum-score conditions and test the next slightly steeper realizable slope, 0.04583 per minute versus 0.045. This probes whether retention can be shortened without pushing the early critical pairs below R = 1.5.

The 60 C optimum is tightly bracketed, so retain injection 6 and explore a potentially wider resolution margin at 45 C. Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 12 to test whether both marginal pairs improve while the last peak remains within 10 minutes.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime, where the central and late near-crossings seen at 35 C may separate again. The strong final organic fraction limits truncation risk, and injection 6 remains the maximum-score benchmark.
Shorten the newly fully resolved 25 C gradient by one grid step to reduce retention. This tests whether its larger minimum-resolution margin can support a faster maximum-score separation.

The steeper 25 C gradient lost central-pair resolution, so restore the successful slope and raise the starting organic fraction instead. This tests a different route to shortening the fully resolved low-temperature separation.

Slightly flatten injection 17’s gradient to recover its sole under-resolved pair while keeping the higher starting organic fraction. The expected retention increase should still leave the last peak within 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction another step while reducing the slope to help preserve the central critical pair. This tests whether the fully resolved low-temperature method can approach injection 6’s shorter elution time.

Lengthen injection 19’s gradient by one step to recover the sole critical pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 6 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Return to the faster 60 C regime and combine a lower starting organic fraction with a steeper gradient. These changes may offset their opposing effects on the critical pairs and reveal a wider fully resolved operating window around injection 6.

Slightly flatten injection 21’s gradient to improve its sole under-resolved early pair, checking whether the later pair retains sufficient separation. Injection 6 remains the fastest demonstrated method with maximum CRF.

Test a substantially higher starting organic fraction to see whether the central pair separates again after an elution-order crossing, potentially yielding a much faster method. Injection 6 already secures the maximum CRF and remains the fallback.

Shorten injection 23’s fully resolved gradient by one grid step, using its minimum R of 1.97 as headroom. This targets an even faster maximum-score separation while retaining injection 23 as the fastest proven method.

Increase the slope moderately to 0.05 per minute, targeting a shorter separation while preserving the two smallest resolution margins. Lowering the endpoint avoids the larger slope jump from shortening tG alone; injection 24 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.
